content:
Critics say the Quran wants it both ways about Muhammad (peace be upon him). It calls him ummī, usually translated "unlettered", yet the first revelation opens with the command "Read", and goes on to say that man was made from "clots". To the critic, a God who orders an illiterate man to read has made a poor start.

Below are five points: what ummī can mean, what 29:48 actually claims, what the first command asked of him, what the word rendered "clots" means, and how the reports of his writing are weighed. Each objection is stated at full strength and then answered from the sources. The article Who wrote the Quran? touches the same word briefly; this one goes further.

The objection assumes that ummī in the Quran means "cannot read". Classical commentators often did take it that way, and some linked it to umm, "mother", as in one who remains as his mother bore him. That reading is old and respectable, and it is the one most translators follow in 7:157-158.[1]

The Quran also uses the plural ummiyyūn for a whole community. In 62:2 God raised a messenger "among the ummiyyīn, from themselves". In 3:20 and 3:75 the word sets the Arabs against the People of the Book, those who already held a scripture. In 2:78 it describes people who know the Book only through wishes. Many modern scholars conclude that the word often means "of the nations without a scripture", a sense that says nothing about any individual's skill with a pen.[2] The two senses are not exclusive, and the Quran never needs to choose. The critic is right that 7:157 alone cannot settle the matter.

The sense "of the nations" has a parallel in Hebrew. Jewish writers spoke of the ummot ha-olam, the nations of the world, meaning the peoples outside Israel who had not received the Torah, and several scholars have suggested that the Arabic ummi reflects the same idea: a person, or a people, outside the communities of scripture.[2] On that reading the Quran's description of the Prophet as the ummi prophet means the prophet sent to and from the Arabs, a people without a previous book.

The clearest verse is 29:48: "You did not recite any book before it, nor write one with your right hand; then the doubters would have had cause to doubt."[3] It is addressed to his own townspeople, who had known him for forty years. A claim of that kind is risky if it is false, because those who heard it could contradict it from memory.

The Quran records what his opponents did say. They charged that a man was teaching him, and the answer given in 16:103 is that the man they hinted at spoke a foreign tongue while this recitation is in clear Arabic.[4] They also charged in 25:5 that he had "had them written down" and that they were dictated to him morning and evening.[5] That accusation is one of dictation to a scribe. The sources record no accusation from Quraysh that he read the text from a page. Note the limit of the argument: 29:48 speaks of books before the revelation. It does not say that he could never, at any later time, form a letter.

His practice in Medina points the same way. He kept scribes, among them Zayd ibn Thabit and Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who wrote down revelation and his letters. When he was told that foreign rulers would not read a letter without a seal, he had a silver ring made, engraved "Muhammad the Messenger of God", and used it to seal the letters he sent.[6] A man who wrote his own letters would have had less need of a staff of scribes. The reports describe a ruler who dictated and sealed.

The first revelation (96:1-5) begins iqraʾ. In the report from Aisha in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Book of the Beginning of Revelation, the angel says "Read", he answers "I am not a reader", and the angel presses him until he repeats the words.[7] The critic reads this as an order to do something he could not do.

The verb qaraʾa means to read, but also to recite aloud, and the Quran itself uses the related noun qurʾān for a recitation (75:17-18).[8] On that sense the command is "recite what is given to you", and the words follow at once: "in the name of your Lord who created". The angel did not hand him a page to decipher. The report also keeps his protest, and the fear he felt on returning to Khadija. A reader may take that as the account of a man surprised by what had happened to him. Whether one takes the story as true or not, it does not describe a test of literacy that he failed.

The Quran reflects on the moment in a later verse addressed to the Prophet: "Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Upon Us is its collection and its recitation."[8] The commentators explain that he used to repeat the words eagerly as they came, afraid of forgetting them, and was told that God would preserve them in his memory. That fits a recitation received and committed to memory. It does not fit a text read from a page.

Verse 96:2 says that man was created "from ʿalaq". Many English translations say "clot", which sounds crude, and critics add that a clot is not what a human is made from. The root ʿ-l-q means to cling or hang on. Classical dictionaries and commentators gave the sense of a clot of blood, and also of something that clings, and some translators now write "a clinging thing".[9]

The same word appears in 22:5 and 23:14 as one stage in a sequence: a drop (nuṭfa), then ʿalaqa, then a morsel of flesh (muḍgha), then bones clothed in flesh.[10] The purpose of 96:2 is to point to the lowly origin of the person who is told in the next verse that his Lord is most generous. Muslim writers differ on how closely these stages match modern embryology, and the article 7 scientific claims about the Quran, graded on the evidence takes up that question. The narrow point here is that the word has a documented range of meaning, and "absurd" is a judgement made after choosing the least generous translation.

The verses that follow also matter for the critic's charge. Having called man to read or recite, the passage says that God "taught by the pen, taught man that which he knew not".[11] The first revelation praises writing as a gift of God, addressed to a messenger who, on the classical reading, did not write. Muslims have often seen the pairing as part of its meaning: the message would be carried by a man who did not write, and preserved by a community that wrote it down.

The strongest evidence for the critic is a report of the treaty of Hudaybiyya. In one wording in Sahih al-Bukhari, in the chapter on the make-up pilgrimage in the Book of Military Expeditions, the Prophet took the document, "did not write well", and wrote.[12] Ibn Hajar observes that the words "did not write well" are missing from the same report in the Book of Peacemaking and from Sahih Muslim, where Ali is the writer and the Prophet only has the phrase erased.[13] Most scholars read the first as meaning that he ordered the text written. A few medieval scholars held that he did write a little near the end of his life, and that this does not contradict the Quran, since 29:48 speaks of the time before the revelation.[14]

This is a real dispute among Muslims, and it should be stated as one. It also shows why the "both ways" charge fails. The Quran claims that he was not a writer of scripture before the revelation, and that is all it claims. The Muslim case for the Quran rests on its text and on the challenge of 2:23, and not on a fixed fact about his handwriting. If a later report showed that he could sign a treaty, the claim of 29:48 would stand as written.

The dispute was once fierce. In eleventh-century al-Andalus the jurist Abu al-Walid al-Baji argued that the Prophet did write at Hudaybiyya, and was accused by some of his contemporaries of contradicting the Quran. He replied that the verse concerned the time before revelation, and scholars from other regions wrote in his support while others opposed him.[15] The episode shows that Muslims argued the question openly, and that the side which allowed some late writing did not think it threatened the faith. Both sides agreed on what mattered: the Quran came to him as revelation and was not drawn from books he had read.

The bottom line

The Quran does not use ummī for one purpose only. It can mean unlettered and it can mean a member of a people without a scripture, and 62:2 favours the second. The strongest claim, 29:48, is about books before the revelation and was made to people who knew him.

"Read" is best taken as "recite", the report itself records his protest, and ʿalaq has a range of meaning wider than "clot". The reports of his writing are disputed among Muslims and do not touch what the verse says. A critic may still doubt the revelation, and that is a fair position, but the charge of contradiction does not hold.

Notes

  1. Quran 7:157-158; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, commentaries on 7:157. Tabari (Dar al-Tarbiya wa-l-Turath edition, Shamela text), commentary on 7:157: vol. 13, pp. 157–162.
  2. Quran 2:78; 3:20; 3:75; 62:2. For the sense "of the nations", see Sebastian Günther, "Ummī", Encyclopaedia of the Qurʾān, vol. 5 (Leiden: Brill, 2006), pp. 399–402, which sets out a range of senses (a member of the Arab people, one without a scripture, one not taught by a scripture) and notes that the Quranic usage does not itself include "illiterate" as such.
  3. Quran 29:48; commentaries of al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir on the verse.
  4. Quran 16:103.
  5. Quran 25:5.
  6. Sahih al-Bukhari 65, Book of Knowledge, report of Anas ibn Malik; compare no. 5872, Book of Dress.
  7. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Beginning of Revelation, the hadith of Aisha; Quran 96:1-5. Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari (Shamela text), vol. 1, p. 22 (Bukhari 3).
  8. Quran 75:17-18; see the lexicons of Lane (qaraʾa) and Ibn Manzur, Lisan al-Arab.
  9. Quran 96:2; Lane, Arabic-English Lexicon, root ʿ-l-q; al-Tabari on 96:2.
  10. Quran 22:5; 23:14.
  11. Quran 96:4–5.
  12. Sahih al-Bukhari 4251 (Book of Military Expeditions, "The make-up pilgrimage"), report of al-Bara ibn Azib, checked on sunnah.com, where the words "he did not write well" appear; Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 7, p. 499 (Shamela text). The Peacemaking versions, Bukhari 2698 and 2699, and Sahih Muslim 1783a, checked on sunnah.com, have Ali write the document and the Prophet erase the phrase; Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 5, pp. 303-304 (Shamela text).
  13. Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari, vol. 7, p. 503 (Shamela text), on Bukhari 4251: the phrase is absent from the Peacemaking version and from Muslim.
  14. Discussed in the commentaries on Sahih al-Bukhari, such as Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari, on the Hudaybiyya report. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 7, pp. 503-504 (Shamela text).
  15. On al-Baji and the controversy over the writing at Hudaybiyya, see Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari, commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari 4251, and Qadi Iyad, Tartib al-Madarik, entry on Abu al-Walid al-Baji.
